scenarioName: Hypoglycemic Altered Mental Status — 'He Just Isn't Acting Right': BLS Scope — Oral Glucose Withheld, Glucagon 1 mg IM

scenarioStory.history: 68-year-old male with Type 2 diabetes and hypertension. He was fine this morning and ate breakfast around 08:00. He took his morning medications as always and spent the day working in the garage, completely skipping lunch. About an hour ago (~14:00) he came inside looking pale and sweaty, confused, and 'just not making any sense.' His wife has not been able to get him to answer her since. It is now almost 15:00. His long-acting Lantus insulin is taken every night before bed; his oral metformin was taken this morning. No trauma, no witnessed seizure activity, no complaints voiced before the confusion began.
scenarioStory.course: Initial Contact: A 68-year-old diabetic on nightly Lantus and morning metformin skipped lunch and has been 'not acting right' for an hour. He mumbles incoherently, does not track the providers, is A&Ox0, and will not follow commands — but his airway is patent, his breathing adequate, and his radial pulse strong. The wife is the entire history: the patient cannot give one, and her SAMPLE points straight at the answer — insulin plus metformin plus a skipped meal. The single scenario-defining action is putting a glucometer on him: BGL is 45 mg/dL. From there the BLS treatment decision is the teaching point. Oral glucose is out — MATC reserves it for a conscious patient with a patent airway, and a man who cannot follow commands cannot safely swallow; putting gel in his mouth is a safety failure, not a treatment. IV dextrose — MATC's definitive therapy for the patient who cannot protect his own airway — is not available to this crew: they have not taken pharmacology and cannot establish IV access. The protocol's own language resolves the impasse: glucagon IM/IN is 'an option for patients for whom IV access cannot be established,' which is definitionally true of a BLS crew. Adult dose is a fixed 1 mg IM/IN. The pale, cool, diaphoretic skin is the protocol's own pertinent finding — diaphoresis may be associated with hypoglycemia — and the heart rate of 112 is the catecholamine response to a starving brain. → Glucagon given: Glucagon works the way its mechanism promises — slowly. It does not deliver glucose; it asks the liver to release stored glycogen, so the first minutes after the injection change nothing, and the airway watch continues: a hypoglycemic patient who has not yet turned the corner can still lose his airway, and oral glucose remains contraindicated until he can follow commands. Then the mumbling organizes into words; he begins looking at the providers and can state his name. Within 15 minutes he is Alert and Oriented ×4, asking 'Wow, I feel a little shaky. What happened?' Repeat glucose during the recovery reads 110 mg/dL; the skin turns pink, warm, and dry; and the heart rate settles to 88. Two protocol details matter here. First, reassessment is a named protocol step, not a courtesy: vitals, mental status, and — because his mentation had not yet normalized when it was drawn — the repeat glucose. Once his mental status has returned to normal, the protocol is equally explicit that further glucose checks are NOT required. Second, what glucagon spent cannot be spent twice: his hepatic glycogen stores are now partly emptied, and the nightly basal Lantus dose is still ahead of him — facts that belong in the disposition conversation coming next. Document what was found, what was given, and what changed. → Recovery confirmed: John is fully recovered, mildly embarrassed, and hungry. Mary offers to make him a peanut butter and jelly sandwich, and he asks whether he really has to go to the hospital. MATC does not leave this to gut feel — it gives an 8-item checklist, release without transport only if ALL are true. Walk it literally: (i) repeat glucose 110 is greater than 80 — pass. (ii) He takes insulin and metformin and does NOT take long-acting oral sulfonylureas — read the words carefully: the criterion excludes glipizide/glyburide-class agents, not long-acting insulin, so Lantus PASSES this criterion as written. (iii) Normal mental status, no focal deficits — pass. (iv) He can promptly obtain and will eat a carbohydrate meal — the PB&J, pass. (vi) A reliable adult (Mary) will stay with him — pass. (vii) No major co-morbid symptoms — no chest pain, dyspnea, seizure, or intoxication — pass. (viii) Clear cause identified — a missed meal, the protocol's own example — pass. Everything therefore hinges on (v): the patient must REFUSE transport AND the EMS clinicians must AGREE transport is not indicated. Offer transport first. If he accepts, he goes. If he refuses, the protocol permits release — and criterion (v) is exactly where the crew's judgment belongs: this recovery was bought with glucagon, which spent hepatic glycogen stores he cannot instantly replace, and the nightly basal Lantus dose is still ahead of him. The source curriculum is explicit that he should be strongly encouraged to accept transport because the glucagon may wear off. Whatever is decided, the performance measure is blunt: if released at scene, the criteria are documented.

scenarioEvents.name: BGL never checked
scenarioEvents.description: The crew never put a glucometer on him — or worse, tried to force oral glucose into a confused man who cannot swallow. Ten minutes later the mumbling has stopped, and not because he improved: he now responds only to a sternal rub with a groan. The untreated sugar has fallen to 30 mg/dL, his respirations have slowed to 10 and gone shallow, his pressure is drifting down at 102/64, and the pulse is 124 and thready. He is at high risk for a seizure, and the quiet patient is the emergency the loud one never was. The rescue now runs through the MATC airway ladder BEFORE the sugar — and every rung of it is BLS: open and maintain the airway with positioning, suction ready, an adjunct sized to his reflexes (NPA while a gag persists, OPA if it is gone), oxygen titrated to 94–98%, and BVM support of his inadequate spontaneous respirations at the protocol's adult rate. Only with the airway and ventilation held does the crew get the glucose it owed him ten minutes ago: check the BGL (30 mg/dL) and give glucagon 1 mg IM/IN — oral glucose is absolutely contraindicated at this level of consciousness, and IV dextrose is out of reach at BLS scope. This patient is critical and transports emergently; dextrose remains the definitive therapy he will get from an intercepting ALS unit or the emergency department. The debrief writes itself: 'not acting right' = check the sugar, and a BGL is a vital sign in every AMS patient.

Check the blood glucose NOW — the vital sign owed 10 minutes ago (reads 30 mg/dL)
Glucagon 1 mg IM/IN — pain-responsive, cannot swallow; no IV option at BLS scope
Reassess and transport emergently — this patient is critical and is not a release candidate
